claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
The high-temperature BCC state is metastable during cooling.
Limited atomic diffusion during cooling induces local chemical partitioning.
Local chemical partitioning triggers nucleation and growth of secondary phases such as B2 or sigma.
Differential elemental mobility, particularly involving chromium enrichment, produces local chemical heterogeneity.
Local composition fluctuations lower the free energy for ordered-phase formation.
Diffusion-driven partitioning transforms the single BCC phase into a mixture of the original phase and secondary phases.
Below approximately 700 degrees Celsius, atomic mobility is limited but sufficient to drive elemental partitioning over observable aging times.
Slow cooling or subsequent thermal aging under diffusion-permitting conditions will produce detectable secondary-phase diffraction peaks.
Slow-cooled or aged samples will exhibit greater microstructural heterogeneity than rapidly quenched samples.
Rapid quenching minimizes atomic diffusion and preserves a predominantly single-phase BCC microstructure.
The proposed partitioning mechanism operates only when cooling or holding provides sufficient time and temperature for atomic mobility.
At extremely rapid quenching rates, the BCC state will persist.
Thermal holds that are too short or too cold to permit diffusion will not activate the proposed mechanism.
